title: Jump Game II
directAnswer: Each value is the max jump length from that index; return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index (reachability is guaranteed). The DP fills minimum jumps per index in O(n²). The optimal greedy treats it as a BFS over levels: the indices reachable in exactly k jumps form a contiguous window, so track the current window's end and the farthest index the whole window can reach; every time the cursor hits the window end you've spent one jump and the window expands. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Greedy BFS levels — current window end + farthest reach
remember.formula:
jumps = 0; curEnd = 0; farthest = 0
for i in range(n - 1):          # stop before the last index
    farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
    if i == curEnd:             # finished this jump's reachable window
        jumps += 1
        curEnd = farthest        # window expands to the next level
return jumps
rules: Think in **levels**: indices reachable in exactly `k` jumps are a contiguous window — BFS over the array, no explicit queue.
Carry **`farthest`** = the furthest index the *current* window can reach, updated at every index you pass.
Carry **`curEnd`** = the right edge of the current level; when `i == curEnd` you've exhausted this jump's reach, so **`jumps++`** and set `curEnd = farthest`.
Loop only to **`n − 1`**, never `n` — landing on the last index shouldn't trigger one extra phantom jump.
You never need to know *which* index you jumped to inside a window — only how far the **whole window** reaches, which is why greedy = BFS here.
The problem **guarantees reachability**, so you don't handle the stuck case (that's Jump Game I).
whenToUse: Minimum steps / shortest path on a line where each position grants a forward range
Reachable-in-k-moves sets form contiguous windows (jump *up to* k)
You want BFS's shortest-path guarantee without building a graph
Only the count of jumps matters, not the exact path
antiSignals: Edge weights vary (cost per jump differs) → Dijkstra, not uniform BFS levels
Jumps can go backward or to arbitrary targets → real graph BFS with a queue
You must return the actual jump sequence → augment with parent pointers
Only feasibility (yes/no), not the count → Jump Game I's single-frontier greedy
remember.takeaway: Jump Game II is BFS in disguise: because 'jump up to k' makes each level a contiguous window, you replace the queue with two integers — the window's end and its farthest reach — and count a jump each time the window flips over. The same level-window trick reduces many 'minimum moves on a line' problems from O(n²) to O(n).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise this as a shortest-path/BFS problem and then realise the contiguous reachability lets you collapse the BFS queue into two scalars — plus whether you handle the off-by-one (loop to n−1) that prevents an extra jump.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting a jump at every index instead of only when the cursor reaches the current window's end, or looping to n and double-counting a jump when the last index coincides with curEnd.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name it as BFS over levels, present the O(n²) DP to show you can model min-jumps formally, then collapse to the O(n) two-pointer-of-windows greedy and justify why scanning a window and tracking its farthest reach is exactly a BFS layer.

problemStatement:
You are given a 0-indexed array of integers `nums` of length `n`. You are initially positioned at `nums[0]`.

Each element `nums[i]` represents the maximum length of a forward jump from index `i`. In other words, if you are at `nums[i]`, you can jump to any `nums[i + j]` where `0 <= j <= nums[i]` and `i + j < n`.

Return *the minimum number of jumps to reach* `nums[n - 1]`. The test cases are generated such that you can reach `nums[n - 1]`.
constraints: It is guaranteed you can reach the last index
From index i you may jump to any index in [i+1, i+nums[i]]
understanding: Starting at index 0, each cell gives the maximum forward hop length. Find the fewest hops needed to land on (or past) the final index. Reachability is guaranteed, so the answer always exists — you only need the minimum count, not the route.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must I jump exactly nums[i], or up to nums[i]?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to — any length from 1 to nums[i]. That 'up to' makes the set of indices reachable in k jumps a contiguous window, which the greedy exploits.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is reaching the last index always possible?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, the problem guarantees it. So unlike Jump Game I, I never return -1 or handle a stuck state.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If the array has one element, what's the answer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0 — you're already on the last index, no jumps needed. The loop-to-n−1 bound handles this naturally.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I overshoot the last index?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, a jump that lands at or beyond n−1 counts as reaching it. We clamp ranges to n−1 in the DP and stop the greedy loop early.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to index 1, then 3 steps to the last index. Two jumps.
Index 0 → index 1 (reach covers up to index 4), then index 1 → index 4. Two jumps.
Already on the last index — zero jumps.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: It's a shortest-path question; contiguous reachability turns the BFS queue into two integers.

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming — Min Jumps to Each Index
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this to show you can model min-jumps formally as a recurrence, then flag the O(n²) range scan as the cost to eliminate.
hints: Let dp[i] be the minimum jumps to reach index i. dp[0] = 0. How does reaching i depend on earlier indices?
From index i you can extend to any j in [i+1, i+nums[i]] with one more jump, so dp[j] = min(dp[j], dp[i] + 1).
Sweep left to right, relaxing each index's reachable range. The answer is dp[n−1].
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of n indices we relax up to its full jump range (length up to nums[i]), so the worst case is O(n²) time; the dp array uses O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Define `dp[i]` = the minimum number of jumps needed to arrive at index `i`, with `dp[0] = 0`. Process indices left to right; from a reachable `i`, every index `j` in `[i+1, i+nums[i]]` can be reached in `dp[i] + 1` jumps, so we relax `dp[j] = min(dp[j], dp[i] + 1)`. The answer is `dp[n−1]`.

**Why left to right works.** To reach `j`, you must have first reached some earlier `i` whose jump range covers `j`. Filling left to right guarantees that when we *use* `dp[i]` to relax forward, `dp[i]` is already final — its value was settled by even earlier indices. So each forward relaxation reads a correct minimum.

**Why we relax the whole reachable range.** A single index `i` doesn't pick one target; it can reach an entire contiguous block `[i+1, i+nums[i]]`, all in one extra jump. To find the minimum jumps to every index, we must offer `dp[i] + 1` to *each* index in that block and keep the smallest offer any predecessor makes. That's the `min` relaxation over a range.

**Why we don't ship this.** That per-index range relaxation is the quadratic cost: with `n = 10⁴` and large jump values, you can approach 10⁸ relaxations. The DP is the honest way to *define* min-jumps and prove the recurrence, but it recomputes information that the contiguous-window structure makes free. The greedy notices that the indices sharing the same `dp` value form a contiguous band — a BFS level — and processes each band in O(1) amortised.

**Why the DP still earns its keep.** Stating it shows the interviewer you can formalise shortest-jumps as a relaxation, and it makes the leap to BFS levels obvious: the set `{i : dp[i] = k}` is exactly the k-th BFS layer, and those layers are contiguous because every reach is an interval.
approaches.insight: The DP reveals the fact the greedy exploits: indices with the same minimum jump count form a *contiguous window*, because each index reaches an interval and intervals union into intervals. Once you see that 'dp[i] = k' carves the array into consecutive bands, you realise you don't need n separate dp cells — just the boundary of the current band.

Each index reaches only the next, so dp = [0,1,2,3]; returns 3.

pitfalls: Forgetting to clamp i + nums[i] to n−1 — out-of-bounds writes on large jump values.
Relaxing from an index whose dp is still infinity — propagates garbage (guard with the continue).
Shipping O(n²) when n = 10⁴ makes the linear greedy clearly preferable.

approaches.name: Greedy — BFS Over Contiguous Levels (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'BFS where each level is a contiguous window, so I replace the queue with curEnd and farthest' and justify why a window scan equals a BFS layer.
hints: Think BFS: level 0 is index 0, level 1 is everything reachable in one jump, level 2 in two jumps, and so on. The answer is the level number of the last index.

Because each index reaches a contiguous range, each level is itself a contiguous window. Track curEnd = the right edge of the current level and farthest = the furthest the whole current level can reach.

Scan left to right updating farthest. When the cursor i hits curEnd, you've consumed the entire current level → increment jumps and set curEnd = farthest. Loop only to n−1 to avoid an extra phantom jump.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single left-to-right pass with O(1) work per index (one max, one comparison) gives O(n) time, and we keep just three integers — jumps, curEnd, farthest — so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Run BFS without a queue. Maintain `curEnd` = the right boundary of the current BFS level (the farthest index reachable in `jumps` jumps) and `farthest` = the farthest index reachable in `jumps + 1` jumps, discovered by scanning the current level. Sweep `i` from `0` to `n−2`, updating `farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])`. When `i` reaches `curEnd`, the current level is fully explored, so increment `jumps` and advance `curEnd = farthest` to the next level's boundary.

**Why this is literally BFS.** Model each index as a node with edges to every index in its jump range. BFS explores nodes in waves: all nodes at distance `k` before any at distance `k+1`, and the first time it reaches the target gives the shortest distance. The set of indices at BFS distance `k` is exactly `{i : min jumps to i = k}`. The crucial structural fact: because a jump goes *up to* `nums[i]`, the indices reachable in `k` jumps form a **contiguous window** `[prevEnd+1, curEnd]` — there are no gaps. So instead of a queue holding individual nodes, the entire level is described by one number, `curEnd`, and we discover the next level's extent with a running `farthest`.

**Why a jump is counted only at `i == curEnd`.** While `i` is still inside the current window (`i < curEnd`), we're examining nodes that all sit at the *same* BFS distance — we haven't spent another jump yet, we're just gathering how far this level collectively reaches. The instant `i` equals `curEnd`, we've examined every node of the current level; to go further we *must* take one more jump, so we increment `jumps` and roll the window forward to `farthest`. Counting a jump per index instead would massively over-count; counting it at the window edge counts exactly one jump per BFS layer.

**Why the greedy is optimal — the exchange/contradiction argument.** BFS is provably shortest for unweighted graphs, but here's the direct exchange argument for why scanning a window and taking its maximum reach can't be beaten. Within the current level `[lo, curEnd]`, suppose the optimal solution jumps to some index `p` in this window and from there reaches index `q`. Our greedy doesn't commit to a single `p`; it records `farthest = max over all i in the window of (i + nums[i])`, which is `>= q` for *every* choice `p` the optimal could make. Now suppose, for contradiction, that the greedy used *more* jumps than optimal to reach the end. Consider the first level where they diverge: optimal reaches some index `x` using `k` jumps. Greedy's `curEnd` after `k` jumps is the maximum index reachable in `k` jumps, so `curEnd >= x` — greedy is at least as far along after the same number of jumps. By induction this holds at every level, so greedy reaches (or passes) the last index in no more jumps than optimal. The maximum-reach window *dominates* any specific sequence of choices, which is exactly why the greedy never needs to backtrack or pick a particular landing index.

**Why loop to `n − 1`, not `n`.** If the last index coincides with a `curEnd`, iterating onto it would trigger one final `jumps++` for a jump we never actually take (we're already there). Stopping at `n − 2` guarantees we count a jump only for transitions that genuinely advance us, so `nums = [0]` correctly yields `0`.

**Why this beats the DP.** The DP recomputes `dp[j]` for every `j` in every range; the greedy notices those values form contiguous levels and tracks only the level boundary plus a running max, collapsing `O(n²)` to `O(n)` and `O(n)` space to `O(1)`.
approaches.insight: The unlock is seeing 'minimum jumps' as 'BFS depth', then noticing that 'jump *up to* k' makes every BFS layer a gap-free interval — so the queue degenerates into two integers. You don't choose *which* index to jump to inside a layer; you only track how far the whole layer can throw you, and that maximum dominates every individual choice. This window-as-level idea is the seed for many 'minimum moves on a line' problems.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop runs for i in range(0) — never executes — so jumps stays 0. Already on the last index.
i=0: farthest=2, i==curEnd → jumps=1, curEnd=2; loop ends (n−1=1). Returns 1.
Levels: [0]→[1]→[2,3]→[4]; cursor hits each curEnd, yielding 3 jumps.

pitfalls: Looping to n instead of n−1 — double-counts a jump when the last index equals curEnd.
Incrementing jumps at every index rather than only when i reaches curEnd.
Overwriting farthest = i + nums[i] without the max — a small later jump shouldn't shrink the next level's reach.

commonMistakes: Counting a jump at every index instead of only when the cursor reaches the current level's boundary.
Iterating the loop to n and double-counting a final jump when the last index coincides with curEnd.
Reaching for an O(n²) DP when the BFS-level greedy solves it in one O(n) pass.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting a jump per index
commonMistakesDetailed.why: All indices inside the current window sit at the same BFS depth. Incrementing jumps for each of them counts steps you never took — the count balloons far above the true minimum.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
jumps = 0
for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
    farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
    jumps += 1            # wrong: counts every index
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
jumps = 0
for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
    farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
    if i == cur_end:      # only at the window boundary
        jumps += 1
        cur_end = farthest

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Looping to n instead of n−1
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the last index equals curEnd, iterating onto it fires one more jumps++ for a jump that never happens — you're already standing on the goal.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Letting a small jump shrink the next level
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Assigning farthest = i + nums[i] without the max can pull the next level's boundary backward when a later index has a tiny value, undercounting reach and inflating jumps.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: farthest = i + nums[i]; // overwrites a bigger earlier reach

patternNote: Canonical 'BFS over contiguous levels' greedy: minimum moves on a line where each position reaches an interval, so each BFS layer is a gap-free window and the queue collapses into curEnd + farthest. Recognise it for min-jumps / min-taps / interval-covering problems; it's the counting sibling of Jump Game's feasibility frontier.
